summary:
Esther is set in the Persian court at Susa under King Xerxes, ruler of "127 provinces from India to Cush" (1:1) — the Hebrew calls him Ahasuerus, generally identified as Xerxes I, who reigned 486–465 BC. Queen Vashti is deposed for refusing the king's summons at a feast, and a kingdom-wide search brings in Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai; her Hebrew name is Hadassah (2:7). She becomes queen while concealing her Jewish identity at Mordecai's instruction. Mordecai meanwhile uncovers an assassination plot against the king; the service is recorded in the royal chronicles but goes unrewarded.

Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman, the king's highest official. Haman is "the Agagite," Mordecai a Benjamite of the line of Kish (2:5) — Saul's tribe and Saul's father's name — and the standoff is often read as reviving Saul's feud with Agag, king of Amalek (1 Samuel 15). Haman obtains a decree to "destroy, kill, and annihilate all the Jews" on a single day, chosen by casting "the Pur (that is, the lot)" (3:7). Mordecai appeals to Esther, though approaching the king unsummoned risks death: "if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place… And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (4:14). She calls a three-day fast and goes — "And if I perish, I perish!" (4:16) — then invites the king and Haman to a banquet, deferring her request to a second. That night the sleepless king has the chronicles read and finds Mordecai's service unrewarded (6:1); Haman, arriving to seek Mordecai's execution, is made instead to lead him through the city square in the king's own robe. At the second banquet Esther discloses her people and names Haman, who is hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai (7:10). Because a sealed Persian decree "cannot be revoked" (8:8), a counter-decree grants the Jews the right to assemble and defend themselves, and they prevail.

God is never named in Esther: the Hebrew text contains no divine name or title and records no prayer (ancient Greek versions added both). The book is often read as providence working unseen — Esther asks for a fast where a prayer might be expected, and Mordecai's "relief and deliverance… from another place" points to a deliverer he does not name. It ends by founding the festival its story explains: the days of deliverance become an annual celebration "called Purim, from the word Pur" (9:26), kept by Jewish communities to this day, and Mordecai stands second in rank to the king, "seeking the good of his people" (10:3).
